extracted.intended_audience: philosophers of mathematics, mathematicians, math educators, and cognitive scientists interested in visualization and diagrammatic reasoning
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards for when and how visual representations (diagrams, pictures, imagery) legitimately contribute to mathematical proof, discovery, and understanding, and what makes visual reasoning reliable or unreliable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-superfluous and non-replaceable visual thinking counts in proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Visual thinking can form a non-superfluous part of the process of thinking through a proof when it is neither merely facilitative (superfluous) nor replaceable by non-diagrammatic thinking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish three possibilities when diagrams appear in thinking-through-a-proof: (a) diagrammatic thinking is always superfluous, (b) sometimes non-superfluous but replaceable by non-visual thinking, (c) some diagrammatic thinking is neither superfluous nor replaceable. The chapter argues that (c) obtains: examples (e.g., Euclid's constructions, Miller's FG derivation) show diagrammatic thinking can be essential and non-replaceable. Use this criterion to judge whether visual steps are epistemically significant or mere aids.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal diagrammatic systems and soundness validate visual proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: If a formal system treats diagrams as syntactic objects and one can demonstrate the system's soundness with respect to an interpretation, then going through diagrammatic derivations in that system constitutes thinking through a proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Miller's FG formal diagrammatic system for Euclidean geometry — a derivation in FG plus a proof of soundness provides a genuine proof where visual reasoning is non-superfluous. Barwise and Etchemendy's programme and Hyperproof are cited as formal approaches. Use the existence of a formalized, sound diagrammatic system as strong evidence that particular diagrammatic reasoning counts as proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Error type (1): relevant mismatch between diagram and textual description
rubrics_metrics.description: Diagrams that represent properties ruled out by the description, or omit properties entailed by the description, produce invalid or misleading reasoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These mismatches are comparatively rare and usually avoidable with care. Example: the famous 'all triangles are isosceles' fallacious diagram where a point is (incorrectly) placed inside instead of outside the triangle. When evaluating a visual argument check that the diagram faithfully represents the construction or hypotheses described in text/caption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Error type (2): unwarranted generalization from over-specific diagrams
rubrics_metrics.description: Visual representations are typically indiscrete: they often represent instances with particular additional features not required by the specification, leading to unwarranted generalizations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dot-diagrams and triangular-number arguments illustrate the risk: a diagram for n=6 may suggest features not holding for all n (e.g., failing at n=1). The evaluator should ask whether a feature seen in the diagram is demanded by the specification or is an accidental artifact of the particular drawing/imagination. If the latter, the generalization may be unsafe.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement of accompanying text or conventions for diagram interpretability
rubrics_metrics.description: A figure alone may be ambiguous; to function in proof or discovery a diagram usually requires accompanying textual instruction or shared conventions to fix its intended interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple interpretability of diagrams can be exploited but also causes hazards. If no text appears, one must assume some background conventions — make those explicit when assessing the epistemic status of a visual argument. When conventions are absent or unclear, downgrade the diagram's evidential force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strict vs relaxed standard for generalization from an arbitrary instance
rubrics_metrics.description: Two standards for valid generalization from a visual instance: the strict option requires an explicit, conscious check that the arbitrary-instance proviso is met; the relaxed option allows generalization if the thinker is sensitive to potential errors and would detect failures in similar cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under the strict option many familiar visual arguments fail (they lack explicit checks). The relaxed option permits visual reasoning provided the thinker has the sensitivity (from experience and vigilance) to detect atypical counterexamples; use deliberative reflective checks or demonstrations (e.g., inductive-style visual checks) to satisfy the standard being applied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reflective checking or formal/inductive justification to secure visual generalizations
rubrics_metrics.description: To turn a visually-intuited generalization into a genuine proof one must make explicit the method exemplified and show (e.g., via base case and inductive step or analytic justification) that the method applies universally, not just to the depicted instance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the triangular-number visual argument can be secured by showing visually that the method works for 2 and that if it works for k it works for k+1, together with reflective reasoning. When such reflective work is absent, treat the visual route as heuristic or discovery rather than proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visual thinking as discovery (reliable belief-formation without full transparency)
rubrics_metrics.description: Visual thinking can produce discoveries: coming to believe a mathematical truth by one's own lights in a reliable, rational way, even if the cognitive processes are fast, unconscious, or sub-personal and lack full transparency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plato's Meno and other examples show that some discoveries arise from hidden activations of dispositions triggered by attentive visual experience. Because processes can be hidden, discovery by visualization often requires subsequent proof to secure and justify the belief for others (or for full epistemic status).

rubrics_metrics.name: Visual thinking as heuristic versus justificatory method
rubrics_metrics.description: Visual representations often serve as heuristics that suggest plausible claims or strategies but do not by themselves justify the claims unless the assumptions invoked by the visualization are checked.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Nelsen's 'proofs without words' can incline the subject to correct conclusions, but conventions of representation might permit counterexamples (curves nearly coincident). Treat unverified visual inferences as heuristics that need analytic confirmation before being accepted as knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations in analysis and limit-based contexts (unreliability with epsilon-delta/limit phenomena)
rubrics_metrics.description: Visual thinking is unreliable for reasoning about limits, tails of infinite processes, and other contexts where epsilon-delta style subtleties matter; some continuous functions (Weierstrass-type) resist naive visual representation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Visual intuitions about continuity, convergence, or oscillatory behavior may be misleading; do not accept visual conclusions about such matters without appropriate analytical justification. Use visualization primarily as intuition or pedagogy in these domains, not as definitive proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: When diagrams are safe: similarity/sameness of class instances
rubrics_metrics.description: If all instances of the relevant class are similar (e.g., all circles, all squares), a diagram will not be over-specific and so can safely support generalization about that class.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify whether the class targeted by the argument admits heterogeneous members that could falsify diagram-based inferences. If class-membership guarantees the diagram's features (e.g., similarity classes), the risk of unwarranted generalization is reduced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof requires derivation + interpretation + soundness
rubrics_metrics.description: A formal derivation alone is a syntactic object and by itself does not constitute a proof; a proof consists of the formal derivation plus an interpretation and a demonstration of the system's soundness with respect to that interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This bears on diagrammatic formal systems too: a diagrammatic derivation must be accompanied by interpretation and a soundness proof to count as a proof. When evaluating purported visual proofs, check whether the link between syntactic diagrammatic steps and the intended semantic conclusions has been established.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visual thinking augments understanding in two senses
rubrics_metrics.description: Visual representations aid (1) grasping definitions, formulas, algorithms, and inference-types, and (2) appreciating why a claim or method is correct (explanatory understanding).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use visualization as a pedagogical and explanatory tool to improve conceptual grasp and appreciation of correctness. However, beware the risks of over-specification and the need for analytic backup in cases where visual intuition can mislead.
